articles.title: Is Sudan’s battlefield shaping the terms of its next political phase?
articles.summary: Army gains, RSF defections and al-Burhan’s political push point to a possible shift in Sudan’s war.
articles.body:
Sudan’s war is showing signs of a changing dynamic. Sudanese armed forces (SAF) have made a series of gains in North Kordofan state; the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces (RSF) is facing a new wave of defections; and army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is opening a political track while insisting the military campaign will continue.

Army advances are putting pressure on RSF supply lines; defections are raising questions about the force’s cohesion; and al-Burhan, who also heads the Transitional Sovereignty Council, is seeking to shape a political process from a position strengthened by developments on the battlefield.

But the wider battlefield remains contested. Together, the military pressure, defections and political outreach point to a potentially important shift: battlefield developments may be starting to affect the political balance.

The clearest recent gains have come in North Kordofan, a state in central Sudan that links the capital, Khartoum, with the country’s western regions.

In late July, the army announced that it had retaken Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala, along with other positions in the state. Al Jazeera reported that the advances also secured the national Exports Road, a key route linking Khartoum, through Omdurman, with el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan.

The gains do not amount to control of the wider Kordofan region. But they have significance beyond the territory captured.

The army’s control of the Exports Road has strengthened its position in North Kordofan and added pressure on RSF supply lines. Al Jazeera reported on August 21 that the army was continuing efforts to cut those supply lines as fighting expanded across Kordofan, Darfur and the Blue Nile region.

The battlefield pressure has coincided with a marked increase in defections from the RSF.

On August 20, the army announced that about 318 people, including four officers, had joined its ranks, arriving in Northern state in about 50 combat vehicles before moving to Omdurman. Al Jazeera also reported separate groups from Kordofan and Khartoum, including 270 people, among them 21 field commanders, as well as 45 fighters and commanders from the Bara area who surrendered to the army.

The numbers alone do not tell the story. The timing does.

Al Jazeera’s August 21 analysis links the growing defections to several factors, including battlefield developments, internal problems within the RSF, social and tribal dynamics, and pressure created by the army’s advances and efforts to disrupt RSF supply lines. It also notes that the trend does not by itself mean the RSF is collapsing.

If the trend continues, it could become increasingly significant, particularly if more commanders and fighters conclude that the battlefield balance is shifting against the RSF.

For now, the more cautious conclusion is that battlefield pressure may be affecting the RSF’s cohesion without yet amounting to a broader breakdown of the organisation.

Why is al-Burhan opening a political track?

The SAF chief’s political initiative is unfolding alongside these military developments.

On August 15, he announced that the state would provide temporary immunity and legal, political and security guarantees to participants in a national dialogue managed by an independent national mechanism. Criminal proceedings against participants facing charges would be suspended during their involvement in the dialogue, without removing the rights of those who had filed complaints.

Al-Burhan said the initiative came from a group of Sudanese who had approached him with a proposal for dialogue. He said the group would independently manage the process and that the state would not determine its agenda or outcomes. He also said he had begun engaging with national forces that had supported the state and its institutions, with the aim of involving them in completing state institutions, including a legislative council.

But this is not a move away from the war.

Al-Burhan said he would not accept what he called a “peace without substance” that would bring RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, and his supporters to power. He also said the path to peace begins with the RSF leaving cities and being gathered in designated areas.

On August 21, Al Jazeera reported that al-Burhan said the fighting would continue until what he described as the rebellion was ended, while the army was working to cut RSF supply lines. He also rejected a truce that would allow the RSF to reorganise, while saying he remained open to a just peace and national dialogue that excluded the RSF.

Al-Burhan is therefore not choosing between war and politics. He is pursuing both, maintaining military pressure while opening a political process he says should preserve the state and its institutions.

Malik Agar, deputy chairman of the Transitional Sovereignty Council, has made the government’s position even clearer.

In an interview with Al Jazeera on August 22, Agar said the current option was military resolution unless serious conditions for negotiations emerged. He said the RSF would have to withdraw from cities and residential areas before negotiations could begin, stressing that the government remained open to initiatives that preserve Sudan’s unity and state institutions.

In a separate Al Jazeera interview published on August 23, Agar said the army would win but that the war would ultimately end through negotiations.

He argued that Sudan’s crisis was rooted in deeper problems, including the weakness of the state and the failure of political elites to manage the country’s ethnic, cultural, religious and geographic diversity.

His position reflects the government’s broader calculation: maintain military pressure while leaving the door open to negotiations from a stronger position on the battlefield.

Can al-Burhan turn battlefield pressure into political leverage?

The army’s gains in North Kordofan have strengthened its position along a strategically important route. The growing defections from the RSF are raising questions about the force’s cohesion. At the same time, the RSF remains active on several fronts, and the wider battlefield remains contested.

That combination gives the recent developments significance beyond individual battles or defections. The changing military balance may now be beginning to shape the terms of Sudan’s next political phase.

For al-Burhan, the potential advantage is not simply territorial. If military pressure continues to produce defections and weaken RSF cohesion, it could give the SAF greater room to shape who participates in a political process and the conditions under which future negotiations take place.

For the RSF, the challenge is therefore not only to hold territory. It is to prevent battlefield pressure from becoming an internal crisis of cohesion.

That has not happened yet. Military setbacks do not automatically translate into political marginalisation.

The army’s recent gains are best understood not as evidence of a decisive victory, but as a shift in the conditions under which the next phase of the war may be fought, and eventually negotiated.

Can the RSF contain the defections and preserve its bargaining position, or will continued military pressure give al-Burhan greater leverage in Sudan’s next political phase?

articles.title: Port Houston donates $500,000 to 32 nonprofits, supporting workforce training, STEM education and community projects
articles.summary: US News: Port Houston has awarded $500,000 in Community Grants to 32 organisations serving communities across the Houston Ship Channel region. The funding will.
articles.body: Port Houston has awarded $500,000 in Community Grants to 32 organisations serving communities across the Houston Ship Channel region. The funding will support programmes ranging from workforce training and STEM education to healthcare access, food assistance, environmental projects and neighbourhood improvements. According to Port Houston press release distributed via Business Wire, the latest grant cycle attracted 194 applications requesting more than $6.6 million, highlighting the scale of demand for community investment. Nearly half of the funding awarded this year is dedicated to workforce development, with supported programmes helping students explore career paths, earn industry-recognised credentials and develop skills for maritime, logistics and industrial careers. Since launching the Community Grants Programme in 2020, Port Houston has invested more than $2.15 million in local organisations. The 2026 awards also mark a transition, with future grants from 2027 set to follow priorities identified through Port Houstonâs Anchored in Action Community Investment Plan.32 organisations receive funding for education, health, food and environmental projectsThe 32 grant recipients represent a broad cross-section of community initiatives. Armand Bayou Nature Center received $15,000 for school field-trip access, while the Barbara Bush Houston Literacy Foundation received $25,000 for East End community STEM literacy initiatives. Baytown Habitat for Humanity was awarded $15,000 for its Safe and Stable Homes Repair & Resilience Initiative, and Art League of Baytown received $7,250 for its Arts and the Ship Channel programme. Compudopt received $25,000 for its Pathways Programme, while Galena Park Resource and Training Center was awarded $25,000 for community learning and engagement. Lee College Foundation received $20,000 for logistics software expansion, linking education directly to one of the regionâs major employment sectors. The grants also address health, food security and access to essential services. Kids' Meals received $15,000 for healthy meal delivery, Second Servings of Houston received $20,000 to expand access to nutritious food, and Target Hunger was awarded $12,750 for food assistance and navigation. Ronald McDonald House Charities Greater Houston received $20,000 for its Care Mobile, while The Rose received $25,000 for its Empower Her Health programme. Other awards support environmental education and neighbourhood improvement, including $15,000 for Citizens' Environmental Coalition, $5,000 for Greens Bayou Coalition and $10,000 for Fit Houstonâs Mason Park revitalisation project.Nearly half of the funding is aimed at building the regionâs future workforceWorkforce development emerged as one of the strongest priorities in the 2026 grant round, accounting for nearly half of the funding. Port Houston said the supported programmes will help residents explore career pathways, gain industry-recognised credentials and develop skills relevant to maritime, logistics and industrial sectors that underpin the regional economy. Several recipients are directly focused on career preparation. SERJobs received $20,000 for its Building the Port Workforce Initiative, Women Offshore Foundation received $25,000 for career development, and the Prison Entrepreneurship Program received $15,000 for workforce and entrepreneurship empowerment. Career-focused projects also include Friends of Galena Park Branch Libraryâs $2,500 Career Exploration and Resume Hub and Friends of Pasadena Public Libraryâs $5,000 programme connecting residents with pathways into industrial construction. Education is another major component. La Porte Independent School District received $15,000 for Elementary STEM Academies, designed to provide hands-on experiences that encourage curiosity, innovation, critical thinking, creativity and collaboration. Houston Symphony Society received $10,000 for its Student Concert Series, while Segundo Barrio Children's Chorus received $20,000 for its community programme. These investments reflect an effort to build skills and opportunities from childhood through adulthood.Port Houston shifts future grants towards community-identified prioritiesThe 2026 awards come as Port Houston prepares to change how its Community Grants Programme is shaped. Beginning in 2027, future investments will be guided by priorities identified through its Anchored in Action Community Investment Plan. The plan was developed using input from more than 10,000 residents across 14 communities located near the port. The change is intended to ensure future investments more closely reflect needs and opportunities identified by residents themselves. That approach builds on the programmeâs existing emphasis on expanding opportunity, addressing community needs and strengthening neighbourhoods connected to the Houston Ship Channel. The latest round also demonstrates how much demand exists among local organisations. The 194 applications submitted in 2026 collectively requested more than $6.6 million, meaning the $500,000 available represented only a portion of the funding sought. Port Houston said the applications demonstrated both the significant needs in the region and the commitment of nonprofits, schools and community partners working to address them. Since 2020, Port Houston has invested more than $2.15 million through the programme. The port also plays a major economic role beyond its grant-making activities, its Houston Ship Channel complex includes more than 200 private and eight public terminals and supports nearly 1.5 million jobs in Texas and 3.37 million nationwide, according to the announcement. The latest grants connect that economic presence with direct investment in education, employment, health, food access, environmental stewardship and neighbourhood development.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Surrogate, California couple clash in court as newborn fights for life after heart surgery
articles.summary: Nausheen Gilkar told a Dallas court her newborn is suffering after open-heart surgery as the surrogate custody fight with McKenna West intensifies.
articles.body: The critically ill newborn at the center of a bitter surrogate custody fight was placed back on a breathing tube after his condition worsened following open-heart surgery, according to newly filed court documents. The baby is in critical condition and being closely watched at the hospital, intended parents Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed said in filings obtained by TMZ. The couple said the child suffered possible complications after a Norwood procedure, an operation used to treat his severe heart defect, and had to be re-intubated after his condition declined overnight. SURROGATE SAYS BABY 'RIPPED AWAY' 60 SECONDS AFTER BIRTH AS CUSTODY FIGHT ERUPTS AFTER ABORTION REFUSAL In a Dallas courtroom Tuesday, Gilkar and Ahmed faced surrogate McKenna West as they fought over who should make medical decisions for the newborn. The clash has drawn national attention because West says she refused the California couple’s earlier request to terminate the pregnancy after the baby was diagnosed with a life-threatening heart condition. Gilkar and Ahmed call the baby Rumi. West, an Alaska cardiac nurse, calls him Gabriel and is asking a Texas judge to give her sole conservatorship, which would put medical decision-making in her hands. HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY Gilkar told the court the couple has been at their son’s bedside as he fights through treatment. She said that since surgery, he has struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and needed a blood transfusion, according to court reporting by The Associated Press. "He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to the AP. She accused West of trying to take him away. "She’s trying to take him from us," Gilkar said. Gilkar described the newborn as "the love of our lives" and said, "He’s suffering a lot." NEONATOLOGIST SOUNDS ALARM OVER MASSACHUSETTS ABORTION LAW ALLOWING PROCEDURES UP TO BIRTH: 'VERY DISTURBING' The custody feud began after the baby was diagnosed at about 20 weeks with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS. West says Gilkar and Ahmed then asked her to terminate the pregnancy. She refused and later traveled to Texas to give birth, Fox News Digital previously reported. HLHS leaves one side of the heart underdeveloped and disrupts normal blood flow. Without treatment, the condition can be fatal within days or weeks, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. AMERICAN RED CROSS DECLARES NATIONAL BLOOD CRISIS AS TYPE O SUPPLY DROPS TO DANGEROUS LEVELS Budner disputes key parts of West’s account and says the couple did agree to the baby’s treatment. He told Fox News Digital that doctors determined on Aug. 14 that the child was eligible for the Norwood procedure, the first of three open-heart surgeries generally used to treat HLHS. Gilkar and Ahmed consented to the surgery, which was performed Aug. 17, he said. At the time, Budner described the baby’s condition as "critical and complex." BOARD-CERTIFIED OBGYN WARNS NEW MASSACHUSETTS LATE-TERM ABORTION LAW EXPOSES MOTHERS TO DANGER West’s lawyers have argued that the court should make sure the baby continues to receive life-saving care. West told the judge she would abandon her custody request if the court determines the intended parents are committed to that care, according to the AP. Gilkar and Ahmed have asked the court to delay a hearing over the temporary restraining order that gave them custody while the legal fight continues, TMZ reported. TWO FAMILIES SUE NORTH DAKOTA HOSPITAL ON ALLEGATIONS BABIES WERE SWITCHED AT BIRTH The custody battle is only one part of the couple’s broader legal fight with West. Before the baby was born, Gilkar and Ahmed filed counterclaims seeking more than $100,000, alleging West breached their surrogacy agreement and caused them emotional distress. The counterclaims, obtained by TMZ, said the couple paid West $60,000 during the pregnancy under an agreement that addressed termination. West has denied wrongdoing and asked the court to dismiss the claims. DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH The dispute has only grown more personal since the baby’s Aug. 12 birth. West said in a New York Post opinion piece last week that she had only about a minute with the newborn, while his umbilical cord was still attached, before he was taken away. A court order has since barred her from seeing or holding the baby. On Tuesday, the judge left that order in place and did not immediately decide the larger question of custody or conservatorship, according to the AP. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency court order before the birth directing that medically necessary care not be delayed or obstructed, Fox News Digital previously reported. Paxton’s office also notified two Dallas medical centers of their obligations to provide life-saving treatment. The Associated Press and Fox News Digital's Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

articles.title: Malaysia’s Anwar puts non-aligned stance in focus with remarks on Taiwan
articles.summary: Malaysian leader’s comments on the island have prompted discussion about whether the country is leaning towards China.
articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s recent comments about Taiwan have raised questions about whether Malaysia is still committed to its traditional policy of non-alignment and not picking sides between China and the United States.

In an interview with Al Jazeera that aired earlier this month, Anwar stated that he saw Taiwan “as part of China, period”, adding that this was “accepted by all”.

More controversially, when asked whether he would condemn China if it resorted to force in the event that peaceful “reunification” did not work, Anwar said that if a Malaysian state were attempting to break away, he would use force to “protect the sanctity and unity of” Malaysia.

Anwar’s comments were praised by the Chinese government, with a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman stressing that Taiwan is “an inalienable part of China’s territory” and that “China must and will be reunited”.

Taiwan’s government condemned the remarks and warned that Anwar’s “one-sided support for China could negatively impact Taiwanese businesses’ confidence in investing in Malaysia”.

Taiwan, the world’s largest chips producer, is a major investor in Malaysia, particularly in the country’s crucial semiconductor industry.

Asked about the issue by local media, Anwar appeared to walk back some of his comments, stressing that Malaysia respected China’s position but favoured a peaceful resolution to tensions in the Taiwan Strait.

Anwar courted headlines again several days after his Al Jazeera interview when he called for the bolstering of Malaysia’s defences in the Bornean state of Sabah.

He pointed to the development of US-backed military facilities in neighbouring Philippines as justification, in part, for increased defence spending.

The Philippine government is in the process of upgrading military facilities on the island of Balabac, 50km (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan.

Balabac was recently added to the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between Washington and Manila, which granted US forces access to designated locations in the Philippines.

Anwar’s comments have bolstered longstanding suspicions among Western commentators that Malaysia is turning against the West and aligning with China, breaking from Malaysia’s traditional policy of non-alignment.

Indeed, Anwar’s remarks come amid China’s growing economic presence in Malaysia, with Beijing now representing Malaysia’s largest trade partner.

Malaysia has also been one of the most enthusiastic recipients of Chinese investment projects, including under China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

Anwar’s seemingly pro-China stance also comes as Malaysia diverges from the West on other geopolitical issues, such as the ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

Long a firm critic of Israel, Malaysia under Anwar has been especially vocal in its opposition to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

However, some analysts push back against suggestions of Malaysia undergoing a strategic realignment.

Chee Meng Tan, an assistant professor of business economics at the University of Nottingham Malaysia, noted that Malaysia’s recognition of Taiwan as “part of China” dates to the 1974 communiqué that then-Prime Minister Tun Abdul Razak signed with Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai to establish diplomatic relations between their countries.

“What was new was Anwar’s statement on the potential use of force, which the one China policy policy does not explicitly require,” Tan said.

Tan notes that Anwar’s comments should also be seen in the context of his upcoming trip to China in September, as he may be attempting to appease Beijing.

Daniel Loebell, a PhD student at Northwestern University in the US who has studied Chinese investments in Malaysia, suggested that Anwar’s position merely represents a realist understanding of territorial integrity.

“Though this idea of violence against Taiwan is immensely troubling to me, I do not think it differs from Malaysia’s policy at all, as he believes that the PRC attacking Taiwan would amount to attacking a rebel organisation within a single state’s own borders,” Loebell said, using the acronym for the People’s Republic of China.

“As head of the government, Anwar sees recognising one government of China amounting to the PRC government’s exclusive right to a monopoly on the use of force within its borders.”

Anwar’s later comments expressing unease over the US-backed base on Balabac can be viewed as linked to Malaysia’s ongoing dispute with the Philippines over the status of Sabah.

The Philippines has claimed Sabah since the territory joined Malaysia in 1963, a claim Malaysia has consistently rejected.

Manila would reaffirm its claim to Sabah in February this year, maintaining that the Philippines’ Maritime Zones Act 2024 preserved its “existing and valid claims” over part of the state.

In July, the Malaysian government lodged a formal protest with the United Nations over the Philippines’ claim to an extended continental shelf, which Malaysia argued encroached on Sabahan waters.

Tan, the assistant professor, argued that Anwar’s comment on the Balabac military buildup may be “a ‘protect-my-border’ reflex rather than a pro-China gesture”.

Anwar’s call to invest in Sabah’s defences also comes as Malaysia seeks to strengthen its defence posture in Borneo, largely to bolster its claims in the disputed South China Sea, where Malaysia is a claimant state alongside China.

While Malaysia has taken a decidedly less vocal stance on the South China Sea dispute than the Philippines, it has nonetheless maintained strong defence ties with Western powers, partly to quietly balance against China’s aggressive military buildup in the disputed waters.

This is demonstrated in Malaysia’s continued commitment to the Five Powers Defence Arrangements (FPDA), a multilateral security framework that also includes Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom.

While not a binding defence treaty, the FPDA commits its members to consult with one another in the event of an armed attack on Malaysia or Singapore. Under the framework, two major exercises are held annually – Bersama Shield and Bersama Lima – involving personnel and assets from member countries.

The FPDA maintains an air defence operations arm with headquarters at a Malaysian Air Force base in Butterworth, Penang, headed by a senior Australian Air Force officer.

Australia also maintains a rifle company at Butterworth and a regular maritime security presence in the region via the deployment of maritime patrol aircraft to Malaysia.

As a central pillar of the FPDA, Malaysia facilitates a Western military presence in the region, which analysts argue provides Malaysia with a quiet deterrent for would-be aggressors.

While Malaysia recognises the benefits of continued defence ties with the West, it also gains from continued Western investment.

As Loebell, the PhD student, noted, Malaysia has “maintained diverse economic relations with many states, and this has kept it from deeply aligning with any major power”.

“The USA still maintains as favourable an economic position as China does,” said Loebell, who doubts that Malaysia is seeking to align more closely with China.

“What’s more, Taiwan’s enterprises continue to invest heavily in Malaysia’s semiconductor industry, and Anwar undoubtedly knows and welcomes this.”

articles.title: U.S. military says it killed four in strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean
articles.summary: The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” almost a year ago.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. military attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its monthslong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America. The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting those it calls “narcoterrorists” almost a year ago. As with most of the military’s statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes. The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed an image of what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash. Tuesday’s strike came just two days after the U.S. military carried out a strike on a vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs. That action came after a pause of more than two months in the U.S. campaign against alleged smugglers. The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in “armed conflict” with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

articles.body: MUMBAI: 'No' has got some stiff competition in Mumbai after the mandatory requirement of working knowledge of Marathi has, of late, seen cab and autorickshaw drivers rushing to polish their language skills. After having picked up basic Marathi at RTO-run language classes, some auto drivers are using their newly acquired vocabulary to rustle up a string of excuses to refuse rides.One auto driver in Kurla has scribbled down what he claims are essential phrases in Marathi to get by. Most of these are different ways to turn down passengers - from "mala jevayla jayche aahe" (I need to eat), "mala lagvi la jayche aahe" (I need to use the restroom) and "mala ghari jaychay" (I need to go home), to "mala gas bharaychay" (I need to refill CNG) and "mala riksha durust karaychi aahe" (I need to repair the auto).The driver's notes aren't entirely dedicated to strategic refusals, though. They include practical phrases such as "hoy, basa" (yes, please sit), "kuthey jaychay?" (where do you want to go?), "to kuthe aahe?" (where is that place?) and "ujvi/davi kade gheu?" (should I take a right/left?). Along with the all-important financial vocabulary of Mumbai's transport ecosystem: "sutte dya" (please give change) and "sutte nahi" (I don't have change).The rush for acquiring Marathi-speaking skills comes as the state has enforced the amended Motor Vehicles Rules that require drivers of all commercial passenger vehicles in the state to possess a working knowledge of the language.However, the fear of a crackdown saw a large-scale protest by a section of non-Marathi-speaking autorickshaw and taxi drivers, who stayed off the roads Monday. As commuters bore the brunt, facing travel disruptions and steep fare hikes, state govt Tuesday sought to reassure transport workers by announcing 161 Marathi language training centres across the state and a dedicated RTO helpline to address complaints of harassment, illegal fines and alleged irregularities during Marathi proficiency checks. Transport minister Pratap Sarnaik said the centres would become operational within the next two to three days.Drivers who fail the on-road tests for Marathi-speaking skills are being given a one-month notice period to learn the language. However, driver unions have sought more time and support for compliance. CM Devendra Fadnavis had said Monday that govt was willing to give more time to learn the language.Sarnaik clarified that drivers would first receive a one-month notice, followed by a three-month suspension period. During this time, no immediate licence cancellation would take place, he said.For Mumbai's passengers, however, the real test of auto drivers' Marathi proficiency may be when "hoy, basa" becomes more common than "mala ghari jaychay".You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Watch: US military's 'lethal kinetic strike' destroys suspected drug boat in Caribbean; 4 killed
articles.summary: US News: The US military carried out a strike on a boat suspected of being involved in drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, a.
articles.body: The US military carried out a strike on a boat suspected of being involved in drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.The US Southern Command posted a video of the operation on X, showing what appeared to be a moving boat followed by a flash after the strike.The military said intelligence had confirmed the vessel was actively involved in drug trafficking, but did not release evidence supporting the claim or provide the identities of those killed.Southern Command said on X, âJoint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists.â It said the vessel was operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean.The latest attack comes just two days after the US military struck another vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing two people accused of trafficking drugs.That strike ended a pause of more than two months in the campaign against alleged smugglers.At least 227 killed in boat strikesThe latest attack takes the number of people killed in US military boat strikes to at least 227 in 68 strikes since the Trump administration began targeting suspected traffickers nearly a year ago, according to news agency AP.The military has described those targeted as ânarcoterroristsâ and has said the vessels were operating along known smuggling routes in the Caribbean and the eastern Pacific.However, the military has generally not provided evidence publicly establishing that the targeted vessels were carrying drugs.In Tuesday's case, Southern Command provided no details about the vessel's cargo or the identities of the four people killed.The strikes have faced criticism from human rights organisations, including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, as well as independent UN experts, who have described the attacks as unlawful extrajudicial killings, according to Reuters.Trump administration expands anti-cartel campaignPresident Donald Trump has said the US is in âarmed conflictâ with Latin American cartels and has defended the strikes as necessary to stop drugs from reaching the United States and contributing to fatal overdoses.The administration has also sought agreements with Latin American governments to expand military operations against criminal groups on land.War secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations on their territory. Guatemala denied reaching such an agreement, while Ecuador launched similar missions with the US in March.The campaign has drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars, particularly over the legal basis for the strikes.The Pentagon's inspector general said in May that it planned to examine whether the military followed its established six-phase Joint Targeting Cycle when conducting the strikes.The review, however, was not intended to determine whether the attacks themselves were legally justified.The strikes have also raised questions over their effectiveness, with critics pointing out that fentanyl linked to many fatal US overdoses is generally trafficked over land from Mexico, where it is produced using chemicals imported from China and India.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Khalistani terrorist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen, claimed on Tuesday (local time) that he had been warned by both the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) of a ânew credible threatâ to his life.Pannun, the general counsel of Sikhs For Justice (SFJ), said FBI agents visited him last Thursday and advised him not to travel until the threat was resolved. He added that the agency asked him to notify them in advance if he did make any travel plans.Also Read | â$100,000 reward for raising Khalistani flags before EU leadersâ: FIR filed against Gurpatwant Singh Pannun ahead of Republic DayâI was warned under the terms of a âDuty to Warnâ law in the United States,â Pannun told the Associated Press, referring to a provision that requires US intelligence and law enforcement agencies to alert individuals when they become aware of credible and specific threats involving murder, serious bodily harm or kidnapping.âIâm not afraid of their death threats. Iâm going to continue, even at the cost of a bullet,â Pannun said.His remarks came after he claimed that the RCMP had also warned him by telephone on Tuesday. Neither law enforcement agency, however, disclosed details of the alleged plot or threat.Pannun further stated that Canadian law enforcement officials had issued similar âDuty to Warnâ advisories to Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another Khalistani terrorist and a Canadian citizen, in the weeks leading up to his assassination in Surrey, Canada, in June 2023.Nijjarâs killing had triggered a major diplomatic row between Canada and India after the then-Justin Trudeau government alleged that the Indian government was involved in the assassination. New Delhi rejected the allegations.In a separate case, Indian national Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in February to federal conspiracy charges over a 2023 plot to assassinate Pannun. Gupta is awaiting sentencing, scheduled for November 20, in a Manhattan federal court.Federal sentencing guidelines recommend that Gupta serve at least 20 years in prison.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: As Intelâs CPU market share falls to 31-year low in the market that analysts call 'ugliest segment'
articles.summary: Tech News News: Intelâs share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. According to a r.
articles.body: Intelâs share in the x86 CPU market for PCs and servers reportedly fell under 70 percent for the first time ever since the year 1995. According to a report by Mercury Research, first quoted by CRN, the Intel numbers mark a 31-year low for the semiconductor giant, even as AI spending fueled historic growth for its data center business. Dean McCarron, president of Prescott, Arizona-based CPU-tracking company Mercury Research, confirmed the point about Intelâs 31-year low to CRN in an email following the release of his second-quarter CPU market share report comparing Intel and AMD.Asked to comment, an Intel spokesperson referred CRN to record year-over-year sales growth for its Data Center Group and momentum in its client business unit touted in its latest earnings report as well as a growing number of long-term supply agreements.As per the Mercury report, Intelâs overall x86 CPU market share fell 6.5 points year over year and dropped by under 1 point sequentially to 69.3 percent as AMDâs position grew just as much to 30.7 percent, a new record for the rival, the researcher said.Market share of Intel and AMD in various sub-segments now stands as follows:* Desktop CPU: Intel at 65.1 percent vs. AMD at 34.9 percent* Laptop: Intel at 71.1 percent vs. AMD at 28.9 percentThese figures were based on total CPU shipments for PCs and servers, not including semicustom, embedded and IoT products. If those latter three segments were included, Intelâs share for the second quarter would stand at 65.9 percent, down 4.6 points year over year and down 1.5 points sequentially, against AMDâs 34.1 percent, according to Mercury.One thing that is said to have helped AMD was "better than expected" shipments of the companyâs system-on-chips for gaming consoles. Unlike AMD, Intel does not have a big console business for its chips.Coming back, in the PC market, AMDâs share grew by 6.4 percent year-over-year to a record 30.3 percent against Intelâs 69.7 percent. What also needs to be noted here is that total desktop PC shipments declined by 20 percent year-over-year in the second quarter.How the 'ugliest' segment of the market faredOverall, the report describes the desktop X86 CPU market as "ugly." Hit by limited availability of graphics cards and high prices of components like motherboards, memory modules, and SSDs, the desktop CPU market was particularly weak in the second quarter and shrunk by over 20% year-on-year (YoY) as well as quarter-over-quarter (QoQ) due to seasonality. According to Mercury Research, both AMD and Intel suffered significant annual shipment declines, but AMD all in all held up better.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: US Court to pharma giant Guardant Health: You willfully infringed patents for cancer-testing; asked to pay $245 million to University of Washington
articles.summary: Tech News News: A federal judge has finalized a judgment ordering pharma giant Guardant Health to pay more than $245 million to Seattle-based biotech startup TwinStra.
articles.body: A federal judge has finalized a judgment ordering pharma giant Guardant Health to pay more than $245 million to Seattle-based biotech startup TwinStrand Biosciences and the University of Washington for willfully infringing on patented DNA sequencing technology. The final order, entered in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, formalizes an initial November 2023 jury verdict against Guardant. In addition to the upfront payout, the ruling guarantees TwinStrand and the university an ongoing 6% royalty on covered Guardant products through the expiration of the patents in March 2033.TwinStrand was spun out of the University of Washington in 2015 to commercialize the platform. Among its co-founders is molecular biologist and oncologist Dr Jesse Salkâgrandson of polio vaccine developer Jonas Salkâwho served as CEO until 2022 and now co-leads cancer diagnostics firm CytoTerra. Since its founding, TwinStrand has drawn backing from prominent venture firms, including Madrona Venture Group, Soleus Capital, and Section 32, the latter of which led a $50 million Series B round in 2021.The dispute centers on 'Duplex Sequencing,' a breakthrough method developed at the University of Washington that increases the accuracy of next-generation DNA sequencing by more than 10,000-fold. By eliminating standard sequencing errors, the technology allows clinicians and researchers to detect ultra-rare genetic mutations critical for early cancer detection and monitoring.The jury found that Guardant incorporated this proprietary technology without a license across 11 diagnostic products and services, including its flagship Guardant360, Guardant Reveal, and Guardant Shield tests. Following the verdict, the Delaware court denied Guardant's motions to overturn the decision or grant a new trial."Duplex Sequencing solved an accuracy problem the sequencing field had worked on for years, and this judgment affirms the juryâs finding that Guardant Health built products on that invention without a license," said Chad Waite, chair of TwinStrandâs board of directors. "We remained steadfast in our conviction that the facts would prevail, and they have."The $245.2 million total includes: $83.4 million in original jury-awarded damages for infringement through June 2023; $119.4 million in accrued royalties; $22.9 million in interest; and $19.5 million in supplemental damages.Guardant Health says that it will appealGuardant Health announced that it will appeal the final judgment from the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware related to intellectual property claims brought against Guardant by TwinStrand Biosciences, Inc. and University of Washington, with execution of the final judgment and collection of potential royalties stayed pending appeal.âWe strongly disagree with this decision and will promptly be appealing for its overturn,â said John Saia, Guardant Health Chief Legal Officer. âWe have full faith in the strengths and merits of Guardantâs intellectual property and R&D and are confident we will ultimately prevail on appeal.âImportantly, the order published regarding the scope of royalties expressly defined the products included as those that existed at the time of the trial in 2023, many of which have been discontinued or significantly upgraded. Based on Guardantâs updated technology the current versions of Guardant Reveal and Shield are excluded from the order and potential royalties. In addition, the company has validated design improvements to Guardant360 and related services that would exclude impact of the potential ongoing royalties in the decision.Guardant remains confident that it did not infringe the asserted patents. Both TwinStrand patents have been preliminarily invalidated in the companyâs ongoing challenges before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Separately, Guardant is pursuing appeals before the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi has launched a sharp attack on the RSS and BJP over the Manusmriti, questioning their commitment to the Indian Constitution. He accused them of historically favouring the ancient text over the document adopted by the country.Owaisi made the remarks during his address at the Jalsa-e-Rahmatul-lil-Alameen at Darussalam .n Hyderabad on the occasion of the 1501st Eid Milad-un-Nabi. He targeted the RSS over its reported opposition to the Constitution drafted by Dr BR Ambedkar and contrasted the organisation's position with that of Muslim freedom fighters during British rule."I am asking those associated with the RSS about Manusmriti. Is it not true that on November 26, 1949, we adopted the Constitution? Yet, four days later, on November 30, a mouthpiece of the RSS published a complaint against it, stating that it wasn't a constitution at all and that it should have been the Manusmriti. They had issues with the Constitution drafted by Babasaheb Ambedkar," Owaisi said.The AIMIM chief also attacked Hindutva ideologue VD Savarkar, referring to his correspondence with the British during his imprisonment in the Andaman cellular jail."Savarkar was in support of Manusmriti. While he was in Andaman jail, he was writing letters to the British, saying, 'I am with you, please release me.' But what were we doing? Allama Fazl-e-Haq Khairabadi was also in jail; he endured hardships but never wrote a 'love letter' to the British. Instead, he issued a fatwa for Jihad against them. Even today, his grave stands in the Andaman as a testament," he asserted.Owaisi further sought to highlight the role of Muslim figures in India's freedom struggle. He claimed that the first prisoner sent to the Andaman Islands was Maulvi Alauddin, the Imam of Hyderabad's Mecca Masjid."Listen, BJP and RSS people, who was the first prisoner in Andaman? It was not your father, grandfather, or ancestor. It was Hyderabad's Maulvi Alauddin, the Imam of Mecca Masjid. He was the first prisoner," Owaisi told the gathering.His remarks come amid an intensifying political confrontation between the BJP and Congress over the Manusmriti and its place in India's social and constitutional discourse.The BJP has recently targeted Congress leader and Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi over his criticism of the Manusmriti. It accused Rahul of making statements that undermine India's traditions, cultural heritage and democratic institutions. Several BJP leaders, including chief ministers, have alleged that Rahul Gandhi's remarks sought to "belittle" India's civilisational values.At an event titled 'Chhatron ki Goonj' in Pune, Rahul Gandhi criticised a passage attributed to the Manusmriti concerning women's independence."This is a direct quote from the Manusmriti, and these words are a shame, because these words should never ever have been spoken," Gandhi said after quoting the passage: "In childhood, a female belongs to her father. In youth, she belongs to her husband. When her lord is dead, she belongs to her sons. A woman must never be independent."Rahul also called for an end to patriarchal structures, telling female students that the country needs to "smash the prevailing patriarchy" to achieve genuine empowerment for women.The exchange has brought the Manusmriti back into the centre of a wider political debate over constitutional values, social equality and competing interpretations of India's cultural and political history.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe doubles down on loose oil ban, then does a U-turn
articles.summary: MUMBAI: FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe on Tuesday declared that a statewide compliance order on the ban on loose edible oil was non-negotiable and th.
articles.body: MUMBAI: FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe on Tuesday declared that a statewide compliance order on the ban on loose edible oil was non-negotiable and the food safety regulator said accepting the demands to relax or cancel would be inappropriate, but the administration did a U-turn an hour later and withdrew the statements.An official said a meeting is scheduled with govt to discuss standard operating procedures and a decision will be made after that.TOI had earlier reported that FDA's ban on the sale of loose edible oil had come up for discussion at a cabinet meeting on Monday. CM Devendra Fadnavis had stressed that govt is seeking a "middle path". "Strict quality needs to be maintained, but at the same time, traditional businesses also need to be protected," he had said.There was also a letter sent to FDA by Edible Oil Merchants Association.Before making a U-turn, FDA said in a statement, "They (retailers) were informed on Aug 18 that their demands to relax or cancel the rules... are not consistent with existing legal and regulatory provisions." It said accepting such demands "would not be appropriate from the perspective of food safety and public health".Mundhe said the prohibition on the sale of loose or unpackaged edible oil is not a newly introduced decision. "This provision has been applicable across the country since 2011, and the administration has issued a statewide compliance order to ensure effective and uniform implementation of the existing law, which must be strictly obeyed." These, too, were withdrawn.The administration provided the examples of Delhi, UP and Tamil Nadu, where such bans are in place. It said Maharashtra had granted temporary and time-bound exemptions or extensions on the sale of loose edible oil from time to time. "This extension was limited up to 2020 and was not a permanent permission," it said.Meanwhile, FDA suspended the license of Ayub's Restaurant in Fort last Saturday over improper storage of food items like eggs at room temperature, failure to segregate and store raw and cooked food, presence of houseflies, and lack of pest control.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.summary: Trending News: For many Indians, scanning a QR code to pay for a cup of chai or a packet of biscuits barely registers anymore. You scan, pay and move on.But for one .
articles.body: For many Indians, scanning a QR code to pay for a cup of chai or a packet of biscuits barely registers anymore. You scan, pay and move on.But for one French woman visiting India, the sheer number of QR codes she came across was a genuine surprise.In a video shared online, she spoke about how different India's everyday payment culture felt compared with what she was used to in France. She already knew about UPI before coming to India, but she hadn't expected to see it being used so casually for tiny, everyday purchases.A cup of chai? There was a QR code.Street food? Another one.An autorickshaw ride? She could pay digitally.Even when buying a snack worth just Rs 20, a UPI payment was often an option.And that seemed to be the part that really caught her attention.âI really didn't expect thisâWhat surprised her wasn't just seeing UPI in big shops or restaurants. It was how far it had spread into everyday life.She spotted QR codes at roadside stalls, small neighbourhood shops, cafes, rickshaws and other tiny businesses. For her, it was one of those small cultural differences that becomes noticeable only when you're actually living through it.âComing from France, this was one of those little everyday cultural differences that made me think, âWowâ¦ I really didn't expect this,ââ she wrote in the caption accompanying her video.ID@undefined Caption not available.ID@undefined Caption not available.The post quickly got people talking, with many Indians pointing out that this has become such a normal part of daily life that most people don't even think twice about it anymore.One person commented that they hadn't used cash in years, while another pointed out that even a Rs 10 roadside tea can now be paid for through UPI.And that's perhaps what makes India's digital payment story interesting. It isn't restricted to shopping malls, supermarkets or expensive restaurants. The same QR code-based system can be found at a tiny food stall as easily as at a large store.UPI has changed everyday paymentsUPI, or Unified Payments Interface, was launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). It allows people to send money instantly through participating apps linked to their bank accounts.Over the years, it has become part of ordinary life in India. Splitting a restaurant bill, paying the neighbourhood shopkeeper, buying vegetables or paying a driver can all happen with a quick scan.The numbers show just how widely it's being used. In January 2026, UPI processed 21.70 billion transactions, worth more than Rs 28.33 lakh crore.So while a QR code stuck to a roadside tea stall might look completely ordinary to an Indian customer, it can still be quite a striking sight for someone seeing this payment culture for the first time.For the French visitor, it was a simple observation from her trip. For the Indians watching her video, it was a reminder of just how much digital payments have quietly changed the way everyday purchases happen.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: US halts visa appointments globally amid Donald Trump's immigration crackdown
articles.summary: US News: The US has paused visa appointments for applicants around the world as the Trump administration launches a global training programme for consular offi.
articles.body: The US has paused visa appointments for applicants around the world as the Trump administration launches a global training programme for consular officers amid its broader immigration crackdown.A US State Department spokesperson said on Tuesday that the department had begun a training initiative at all US embassies and consulates worldwide. Visa appointment schedules will be adjusted to accommodate the training, the spokesperson said, according to Reuters.The State Department did not provide details on the training or specify how long the adjustments would last.It said the programme was aimed at helping consular officers screen applicants who could potentially become dependent on US public benefits and ensure that visa applications are evaluated "comprehensively and consistently".According to a Financial Times report, immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates had received emails informing them that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would be notified of new dates.The development comes as President Donald Trump's administration continues a broad immigration crackdown that has included visa and green-card revocations and the rejection of applications on various grounds, including political opinions and participation in pro-Palestinian protests.Trump has said the crackdown is intended to improve domestic security.Immigration crackdown faces legal challengesThe administration's immigration policies have also faced legal setbacks. A US judge on Friday struck down a policy that suspended the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, ruling that the measure exceeded secretary of state Marco Rubio's statutory authority.The administration has also moved to tighten restrictions on legal immigration.The US Department of Homeland Security has proposed making permanent a $103,265 fee for new cap-subject H-1B visa petitions, after a previous $100,000 fee imposed by Trump was blocked by a court.The proposed fee would significantly increase the cost for employers hiring foreign workers in specialised fields.The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers with specialised training. The programme provides 65,000 visas annually, along with another 20,000 for workers with advanced degrees.Trump's administration has also ordered enhanced vetting of H-1B applicants and proposed changes to the visa selection process that would favour higher-skilled and better-paid workers.Visa revocations add to pressure on applicantsThe administration is separately preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of potentially up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for or are currently seeking asylum in the US.The proposed action would cover B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought or are seeking asylum. The State Department is expected to announce the move in the coming weeks, according to news agency AP.B1 visas are generally issued for business travel, while B2 visas are generally used for tourism, family visits or medical treatment.The administration has also tightened screening requirements for visa applicants, including demands for additional information about their social media histories and, in some cases, expensive visa bonds.The latest pause in appointments therefore comes as the Trump administration continues to review and tighten several aspects of the US immigration and visa system.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: College student fatally shot by police after knocking on wrong door
articles.summary: Glenn Pysher was trying to find his friends when he accidentally knocked on the door of the wrong house. The homeowners called 911 to report an attempted bre...
articles.body:
A 22-year-old college student was fatally shot by police over the weekend after he accidentally knocked on the wrong door of a home in Pennsylvania, and now his parents are demanding answers.

Glenn Pysher, known to his family and friends as Bubba, spent Saturday night celebrating with friends at a local bar in Upper Pottsgrove, Pennsylvania. When the group decided to move the party to a house nearby, Pysher walked there alone and mistakenly knocked on the wrong door.

His mother, Erin Pysher, said she thinks he got "mixed up" because the house is in a wooded area.

The homeowners called 911 to report an attempted break-in. Police arrived early Sunday and found Pysher in the back of the home.

"So he probably was knocking, 'Hey, let me in, where are you at, what are you doing?' And the homeowners thought he was trying to break into the house and called the cops," his mother told CBS News about what she thinks happened.

There, the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office said, an encounter ensued, and Glenn Pysher was shot and killed. The Upper Pottsgrove Police Department has not released any information about the shooting, but said the incident was under investigation.

"At 12:32, we have the call log, he was talking on the phone with his friends," his mother told CBS News. "By 12:35, I believe, the cops had already shown up and shot him."

"No Taser. No nothing. Automatic deadly force," she said, adding that the family hasn't heard anything from the police department. The Montgomery County Detective Bureau did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.

"I just want things to be done right. I want to know the facts," his father, Glenwood Pysher, said.

Erin Pysher says her son loved playing baseball, and he was looking forward to playing at Saint Elizabeth University in Florham Park, New Jersey, where he recently transferred.

"I was going to take him to school and help him set up his dorm room. He was supposed to start classes on Monday," his mother said. "It's unreal. I don't even know how to explain it. It's a feeling of so much sadness in my heart. I can't — it's hard to breathe."

"He was such a good kid," Glenwood Pysher told CBS News. "The community here loved him, and nobody can believe this happened to this young man who wouldn't hurt a fly."

articles.title: Gao Zhen: China jails artist over satirical Mao Zedong sculptures, say rights groups
articles.summary: The case against Gao Zhen, who was prosecuted under a law banning "slander of heroes", has been seen as an assault on artistic freedom.
articles.body:
A Chinese artist known for his satirical sculptures of Mao Zedong has been handed a maximum three-year jail term for "slandering China's heroes", according to rights groups.

A court in Hebei province had ruled on Tuesday that Gao Zhen's work "infringes upon the hero's reputation and harms public interest".

Among the 70-year-old's most famous pieces, produced with his brother Gao Qiang, is a sculpture comprising a squad of Mao-like figures holding Jesus Christ at gunpoint.

Gao has been in detention for the past two years, and the UN and many rights groups have called for him to be released. Amnesty International has called his sentencing an "assault" on artistic freedom.

Gao had moved to the US in 2022 but was arrested at his studio on the outskirts of Beijing during a visit in August 2024.

Authorities seized his artworks and barred his wife and seven-year-old son from leaving China.

China watchers have said that Gao Zhen's arrest shows how the Chinese Communist Party is becoming increasingly extreme in both grasp and reach – including by policing its citizens transnationally and retroactively.

He was charged under a law that came into force in March 2018, which bans the defamation of historical figures associated with the party.

The Gao brothers' Execution of Christ sculpture was exhibited in 2009, as were two other sculptures cited in the case.

They are Mao's Guilt, a life-sized replica of the leader kneeling in a pose of solemn contrition; and Miss Mao which depicts him with large breasts and a long, Pinocchio-style nose.

Gao's case was heard in a one-day, closed-door trial earlier this year, which received limited coverage in China.

He plans to appeal the conviction, Amnesty International said on Tuesday.

If the verdict is upheld, Gao would be due to complete his sentence in August 2027 as it would take into account the two years that he has already spent in detention.

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty International's China Director Sarah Brooks said on Tuesday.

"This trial demonstrates how broadly worded and politically motivated laws are used – and worse, in this case, used retroactively – to silence artists, activists and other individuals who dare to express views that differ from those of the Chinese government," she said.

"The case against [Gao Zhen] raises particular concerns with regard to the retroactive application of criminal law, the use of criminal sanctions to punish artistic expression, and the impact on his family," the UN's Human Rights Office told AFP news agency.

Earlier this year, his brother Gao Qiang told the BBC that the trial's "message is clear".

"Even if a work was made 15 years ago, it can still be turned into a crime if today's political climate changes," he said.

articles.body: VIJAYAWADA: âHarassment by Sadhik Khan was the reason for my death,â a 34-year-old woman allegedly wrote in a suicide note before jumping into the Godavari river with her parents and 10-year-old son in Andhra Pradeshâs Rajahmundry, police said.The woman, Kovvuri Soujanya, also accused Khan, a rifle shooting coach, of killing her husband, Jagadeesh Reddy, by allegedly administering chemical poison.Soujanya, her parents Tillapudi Nookaraju and Tillapudi Meena, and her son Riyansh Karthikeya Reddy jumped from the Road-cum-Railway Bridge near Rajahmundry on August 17.The boy survived after becoming trapped in the bridgeâs grill before falling into the river. Two fishermen, alerted by police, rescued him. Soujanya and her parents were swept away and their bodies were later recovered.Police have now arrested Khan in connection with Jagadeesh Reddyâs alleged murder.Family travelled from KakinadaThe family had travelled from Kakinada to Kovvur before reaching the bridge late on August 17.Nookaraju, 61, was an assistant engineer in the Panchayati Raj department in Pithapuram in Kakinada district. His wife Meena was 59, while Soujanya was 34.According to police, Nookaraju and Meena jumped into the river first. Soujanya then followed with her son.At around 11.40pm, Rajahmundry II Town Police received a call through the 112 emergency service.Officers who reached the bridge found the family's car and footwear initially assuring Soujanya that he would help her.He then accused Khan of threatening Soujanya, her son and himself with death.Nookaraju also alleged that Khan had taken control of valuables and bank accounts belonging to the family.Mother alleged property plotMeena's note also contained allegations against Khan.She allegedly said she was worried about what would happen to her daughter and grandson and referred to her husband's poor health.She described Khan as cruel and said the family could not face him.She also alleged that Khan would âsellâ her daughter and grandson.Meena further claimed that she had heard a telephone conversation in which Khan allegedly said he would acquire the family's entire property once it was transferred into Soujanya's name.Police are investigating these allegations.Khan arrested in MeerutKakinada district superintendent of police G Bindu Madhav formed a Special Investigation Team to investigate the case.The SIT is being led by Kakinada in-charge sub-divisional Police Officer and Additional SP (Admin) Dr Mahanti Kishore Kumar.A special team travelled to Meerut after receiving information about Khan's whereabouts.With the help of Uttar Pradesh Police, officers arrested him near Nauchandi Police Station at about 9am on August 22.Khan was produced before a chief judicial magistrate court in Meerut, where police obtained articles.title: 12-year-old hailed âheroâ for calling 911 before Montana gunman killed her, 7 others
articles.summary: US News: A 12-year-old girl called 911 from inside a Montana home as a gunman killed eight relatives, including four children, during a Sunday family dinner ou.
articles.body: A 12-year-old girl called 911 from inside a Montana home as a gunman killed eight relatives, including four children, during a Sunday family dinner outside Billings. The victims belonged to four generations of the same blended family.Charlotte Ghekiere, 12, was among those killed. Family friend Jennifer Mercer said the girl called 911 and tried to save her relatives, something the family wanted made public. âThe one thing we do know is that Charlotte was the hero,â Mercer said.The gunman was identified by relative Brad Ireland as Alan Smith, 44. Smith had lived with his parents for years before they asked him to leave a couple of weeks earlier, but he returned unexpectedly on Sunday evening as relatives gathered for their regular family dinner and opened fire, Ireland said, according to news agency Associated Press.Victims spanned four generationsThe oldest victim was Smithâs grandmother, Evelyn Smith, who was in her 90s, used a wheelchair and lived in a nearby retirement community. The youngest was 7-year-old Chloe Ireland.Smithâs parents, Dana and Barb Smith, and his younger sister, Megan Ghekiere, were also killed. Meganâs children with former husband Brad Ireland, Owen Ireland, 13, and Chloe, were among the four children who died.Her two stepchildren with current husband Adam Ghekiere, Landon Ghekiere, 15, and Charlotte, 12, were also killed. Mercer, who was authorized to release information about the victims, later launched an online appeal to help the family meet funeral and other expenses.She described the family as close and loving, saying the children got along and their parents remained amicable even after divorcing. She also said the deaths had devastated the wider community, including people who had never known the family.Officers heard shots before flames engulfed houseOfficers arrived at the property on Sunday evening and heard gunshots from the rear of the house. Soon afterwards, flames engulfed the building.Investigators confirmed on Tuesday that eight people had been killed, including four children. They also said the suspect had suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound and later died. Ireland said Smith killed his grandmother, parents, younger sister and the four children before setting the house on fire. He added that Smith tried to flee before encountering law enforcement.Firefighters could not immediately tackle the blaze because authorities first had to secure the scene. Once they were able to enter the area, crews continued fighting the fire until about 1am on Monday, Billings Fire Department Chief Matt Hoppel said.The subdivision is outside Billings city limits and is not required to have fire hydrants. The delay in starting firefighting operations gave the flames additional time to spread through the house.Family moved to Montana from Seattle areaThe family originally came from the Seattle area. After Ireland and Megan divorced six years ago, she moved to Montana with their children, where she later met Adam Ghekiere, who became her second husband.Her parents, Dana and Barb Smith, subsequently followed her to Montana and settled in Billings nearby. Danaâs elderly mother, Evelyn, lived separately in a retirement community in the area, Ireland said.Alan Smith had also been living in Montana with his parents for several years before they recently asked him to leave. He returned to their home on Sunday evening while relatives were gathering for their regular family meal.Adam Ghekiere was at work and was not at the house when the shooting occurred.Relative says there were âmany red flagsâIreland, who lives in Arizona and lost his former wife and two children in the shooting, said there had been warning signs involving Smith.âThere were many red flags and many people spoke out,â he said. âNo one listened.âHe described Smith as a âhermitâ who generally remained in his room and spent much of his time on a computer. Ireland said relatives did not know what he did there throughout the day.Smith attended Eastern Washington University but had been unable to find a job or keep one. Criminal-record checks in Montana and Washington also found no previous arrest or criminal charge involving him.Ireland said he was unaware of any previous violence by Smith, although he said his former brother-in-law could be verbally abusive.Friends of the victims have since created two GoFundMe campaigns to support Adam Ghekiere and his former wife, Erica Schneider.Montana case is 22nd US mass killing this yearThe case is the 22nd US mass killing recorded this year by a database compiled by the news agency and USA Today with Northeastern University. Of those incidents, 15 stemmed from domestic disputes.James Alan Fox, the Northeastern University criminologist responsible for the database, said domestic disputes account for about half of US mass killings on average.No US mass killing since April has had a higher death toll. In that earlier Louisiana case, a father killed eight children, seven of them his own, and wounded his wife and another woman.Husband raced home after hearing shooting alertAdam Ghekiere was working at the Billings airport when he heard a report of an active shooting over a dispatch radio. He immediately called each member of his family before driving across Billings to the Smith home.By the time he arrived, the house was already ablaze. About two hours later, he learned that his wife and children had been killed.Ghekiere said he had not expected his children to be at the gathering because the family normally held its dinner on Fridays. Their presence that Sunday also led him to believe Smith had not expected to find them there.âI donât think he expected my kids to be there,â he said, referring to his brother-in-law.Police later told Ghekiere that Charlotte had made the emergency call from inside the house. As he recalled his daughter, he said one particular exchange continued to stay with him.âI keep hearing her quote to me every time I would say âI love youâ and she would say âI love you more,ââ he said.Fire damage complicates investigationThe fire burned the house to its foundation, leaving investigators with concerns about the structural integrity of what remained. Those concerns have complicated the investigation, Billings Police Department spokesperson Jeff Stovall said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
